questions.prompt: Why is tool poisoning considered a supply-chain-style attack, worse than ordinary prompt injection?
options: It requires physical access to the host machine
It only affects open-source models
It arrives through a third-party server you chose to integrate, poisoning a trusted channel rather than a single user input
It bypasses TLS encryption entirely
questions.explanation: Lens' MCP Security threat model frames poisoned tools as supply-chain attacks: trust flows from an integrated dependency, not one-off user text.

questions.prompt: In MCP, what does the SAMPLING primitive let a server do?
options: Compress tool outputs before returning them
Rate-limit client requests across sessions
Randomly select which tools stay enabled
Request LLM completions through the client during a tool flow
questions.explanation: Web Dev Simplified's Ultimate MCP Crash Course covers sampling as the client-side primitive intro videos skip: servers ask the client's LLM to generate completions.

questions.prompt: Which defense bundle matches the roadmap's guidance for securing MCP servers?
options: Auto-update servers without review to patch quickly
Allow broad write access but log all calls
Trust the model to refuse malicious instructions
Pin version plus content hash, default read-only, re-approve after changes, sandbox execution, validate responses before context
questions.explanation: The Pillar 8 gap-fill lists pinning (version + hash), read-only default, re-approval after changes, sandboxing, and validating responses pre-context (SentinelOne guide).

questions.prompt: A rug pull (or line jumping) attack occurs when...
options: A server drains funds from a connected crypto wallet
Tool behavior or descriptions change maliciously AFTER user approval
The client downgrades to an older protocol version
Two servers claim the same tool name simultaneously
questions.explanation: OWASP Foundation's MCP Tool Poisoning write-up covers rug pulls: approved tools silently turning malicious later - hence re-approval after any change.

questions.prompt: Which resource teaches building a production-ready MCP server with FastMCP and auth?
options: Google Cloud Tech - How MCP actually works
Microsoft - MCP for Beginners repo
codebasics - Production-Ready MCP Server in 90 min
CampusX - MCP Trilogy playlist
questions.explanation: codebasics' 90-minute video builds a production-grade server using FastMCP with authentication; Google Cloud Tech and CampusX cover concepts instead.

questions.prompt: Which Udemy option explicitly covers OAuth 2.1 for MCP development?
options: Nikolai Schuler - Complete MCP Developer Guide
Ed Donner - Agentic AI Engineering
Andrew Ng - Agentic AI
Krish Naik Bootcamp
questions.explanation: Nikolai Schuler's Complete MCP Developer Guide covers OAuth 2.1; Eden Marco's MCP Crash Course is the alternative that includes security.

questions.prompt: Why do traditional metrics like BLEU and ROUGE fail for RAG and agent evaluation?
options: They require GPU acceleration unavailable in CI
They were patented and cannot be licensed
They measure wording overlap, not whether answers are grounded in retrieved facts
They only work for translation tasks in non-English languages
questions.explanation: The Pillar 9 gap-fill says BLEU/ROUGE measure wording, not grounding - RAGAS replaces them since no human labels are needed.

questions.prompt: What is RAGAS's key practical advantage over classic reference-based metrics?
options: It needs no human-written labels or golden answers
It trains a custom judge model per project
It runs only on proprietary APIs
It eliminates the need for retrieval entirely
questions.explanation: Logical Lenses' RAG Evaluation, RAGAS explained shows faithfulness plus context precision/recall computed without human labels - runnable locally per Analytics Vidhya.

questions.prompt: For evaluating agent behaviors, what scoring style does the roadmap recommend over a vague 1-10 LLM-judge score?
options: Average star ratings across many runs
A percentage similarity score against a gold answer
No scoring at all - ship and monitor
A rubric with a binary pass/fail score per behavior
questions.explanation: Per Andrew Ng's Agentic AI Module 4 guidance echoed in the gap-fill, binary rubric scores per behavior beat vague 1-10 judge ratings.

questions.prompt: According to Andrew Ng, what is the single biggest predictor of agent-building success?
options: Evaluation-driven development
Fine-tuning base models first
Using the largest available model
Multi-agent architectures everywhere
questions.explanation: The Pillar 9 goal cites Andrew Ng: evaluation-driven development is the single biggest predictor of agent-building success (Module 4).

questions.prompt: In RAG evaluation, how should you correctly split your measurement concerns?
options: Score everything with one overall accuracy number
Measure faithfulness for generation grounding separately from context precision/recall for retrieval
Evaluate only final outputs and ignore retrieved chunks
Let the LLM self-report correctness percentages
questions.explanation: Logical Lenses' RAGAS video separates retrieval quality (context precision/recall) from generation quality (faithfulness) - measure each independently.

questions.prompt: How should a RAGAS harness fit into your development workflow?
options: Run once before major releases only
Delegate evaluation to end users via feedback forms
Treat it like unit tests running in CI on every change
Skip it when prompts feel subjectively good
questions.explanation: The gap-fill says treat RAGAS like unit tests in CI on every change; the RAGAS tutorial write-up shows a local no-API setup.

questions.prompt: Andrew Ng's Agentic AI Module 4 covers which evaluation trio flagged KEY in the roadmap?
options: Chunking, embedding, reranking
Objective metrics vs LLM-judge, error analysis, traces
LoRA rank, alpha, dropout
OAuth scopes, tokens, refresh flows
questions.explanation: Module 4 of Andrew Ng's Agentic AI course covers objective vs LLM-judge evals, error analysis, and trace inspection - marked do-not-skip.

questions.prompt: When debugging why an agent failed mid-run, which tool does the roadmap point to for inspecting step-by-step traces?
options: Zep
Mem0
LangSmith
ColBERT
questions.explanation: LangSmith docs provide tracing and observability walkthroughs to inspect each node's inputs, outputs, and errors during a run.

questions.prompt: Within the OWASP Top-10 for LLMs, where does RAG security primarily live?
options: LLM03 Supply Chain
LLM08 Vector & Embedding Weaknesses
LLM09 Misinformation
LLM05 Improper Output Handling
questions.explanation: The roadmap notes LLM08 Vector & Embedding Weaknesses is where RAG security lives - tie it back to Pillar 3; Giskard's overview lists all ten risks.

questions.prompt: Which OWASP risk maps directly to agent and MCP deployments?
options: LLM06 Excessive Agency
LLM02 Sensitive Info Disclosure
LLM04 Data & Model Poisoning
LLM07 System Prompt Leakage
questions.explanation: Per the roadmap, LLM06 Excessive Agency is the agent/MCP risk - granting tools more autonomy than needed - tie it back to Pillar 8.

questions.prompt: LLM07 System Prompt Leakage refers to:
options: Prompts exceeding maximum token limits
System prompts being exposed, revealing instructions meant to stay private
Losing prompt history during application restarts
Encoding errors in multilingual prompts
questions.explanation: Giskard's OWASP Top-10 for LLM 2025 overview counts system prompt leakage among the ten risks: private instructions leaking to end users.

questions.prompt: LLM10 Unbounded Consumption best describes which failure mode?
options: Unlimited free-tier usage granted by accident
Models consuming their own hallucinated outputs recursively
Context windows growing beyond hardware limits
Runaway inference costs or resource exhaustion from unchecked usage
questions.explanation: Giskard's overview defines Unbounded Consumption as uncontrolled resource use - cost and denial-of-service exposure when queries go uncapped.

questions.prompt: Prompt injection (LLM01) comes in two delivery forms. Which pair is correct?
options: Verbal and written
Batch and streaming
Direct (user-crafted) and indirect (hidden in content the model reads)
Local and cloud
questions.explanation: IT Bulls' OWASP LLM01 explained distinguishes direct injection typed by users from indirect payloads planted in documents, emails, or web pages.

questions.prompt: Improper Output Handling (LLM05) occurs when:
options: An LLM's untrusted output is passed downstream without validation - into shells, SQL, or browsers
Outputs exceed temperature sampling bounds
Responses arrive slower than the SLA allows
Streaming responses drop mid-generation
questions.explanation: The OWASP Top-10 Practical Guide flags treating model output as trusted code or query input - sanitize before executing downstream.

questions.prompt: LLM03 Supply Chain covers compromises in:
options: Network cables and routers
User session cookies
Third-party components - packages, plugins, pre-trained models, or fine-tuning data
Browser cache storage
questions.explanation: Ali Dorri's OWASP Top-10 deep dive places vulnerable dependencies and tainted models under Supply Chain - distinct from LLM04 training-data poisoning.

questions.prompt: Why does the roadmap call learning only prompt injection the biggest gap in typical LLM security study?
options: Injection videos are usually too long
Nine other named risks remain uncovered beyond injection
Injection only matters for chatbots
The topic needs mathematics most learners lack
questions.explanation: One injection video leaves 9 of 10 risks uncovered; Giskard's 4-minute OWASP Top-10 for LLM 2025 overview names all ten, LLM01 through LLM10.
